transcription.text: All right, well, welcome back to NeoCloud in SF.
So my name is Steve Ho.
I'm the head of research at Silicon Data.
And I have the great pleasure of interviewing Liran
from WACA.
So for those in the audience who are not familiar,
can you just sort of say a few words about what WACA is
and does?
- Yeah, so at WACA, we deliver the best storage
and memory platform for AI and GPU compute.
And what we're doing,
we're delivering the most performant, scalable,
but also cost performance, very large storage system.
And we used to be very successful
with a lot of these companies running very large training.
And now we're seeing the quite strong shift towards inference.
And by the way, WACA is pronounced like a Greek unit.
- Okay.
- And it's a very big number.
So it's 10 to the power of 30.
So it's like a trillion--
- Not quite as Google, but WACA.
- Yeah, but Google is also not the right word.
It was almost.
And it's like a trillion X or a million Yota.
So it's a huge, huge, huge amount of capacity.
- Enormous, and can I hazard a guess
that the official color of WACA is purple?
- Yes, we really like purple.
- Love it, my favorite color too.
So you co-founded WACA more than a decade ago,
long before the word NeoCloud,
which I don't know how you feel about, became fashionable.
How did you see the AI data infrastructure come?
And how has this market evolved
since the day when you founded the company?
- All right, so we started WACA early '14,
you could call it late '13.
We couldn't convince anyone.
We actually imagined what's going on today.
But we saw three things coming.
Containers with a very big push for microservices started.
So you could fundamentally think
about new ways of building software.
NVMe started happening so you could connect flash
to servers on-premises and the cloud in a common way.
And the network finally caught up to the server.
And actually fast network is also what's allowing us
to run these very large clusters like we do today.
And we said, hey, with these big technology shifts,
we can build fundamentally different storage product.
We did that, took us a few years to make it to market.
And then even though we didn't plan for it,
our first customers were using GPUs back in 2017, 2018.
They didn't call it AI yet,
but they were calling it machine learning, deep learning.
They were solving autonomous driving,
dictation, other autonomous problems questions back then.
And we kept saying, hey, there's great money in that.
That's not what we planned for,
but let's take this detour and work with these crazy GPU guys
as long as the money is good.
So we kept doing it for a few years.
We kept better and better
at supporting these crazy GPU guys.
Up until like back in 2023, the GPT moment happened.
Then everyone started calling it AI.
And now we don't say it's a detour.
This is like what we do.
- So a big theme today, and something I alluded earlier
is the fact that AI has now shifted very rapidly away
from training towards much more about inference.
How do you think that impacts the way AI infrastructure
has been built, so to speak, the crazy GPU guys?
What are they asking you for now?
- It's about what's the biggest, craziest thing
you can build to help you win.
And there is almost no question of economics or even reason,
because they're now, depending how you count it,
between dozens and hundreds different AI labs
that build models, but looking at the horizon,
there wouldn't be so many.
So no matter what you're trying to win at,
only one or two or three players would win at,
and you have to be the best at the end.
And spending is not a problem,
because if you don't end up making it to the end,
it all didn't matter.
So with training, you need to build like,
it's like a formula one.
You need to build the best car, the biggest,
like making it from A to B in the fastest way
and allow them to train.
Inference is a fundamentally different problem.
Inference is how everyone is actually making money
out of AI, how do you actually make it in production?
It needs to be scalable and you have to make ends meet.
So inference is about economics.
Inference is about how much am I paying for the power?
How much am I paying for the capital?
How much is the overall OPEX cost?
And then how valuable are the tokens that I'm delivering
and how many tokens I can deliver?
So it's a fundamentally different question.
People that do it well,
solve it in a fundamentally different way.
>> So to follow up on that question and generally curious,
Waka runs in many near clouds and they did air builders.
Without sharing anything confidential,
would you be able to tell us like what differentiates
the near clouds that succeed and the ones that
like your estimation may not be able to make it in the end?
>> On the one hand, you can say all the near clouds
should be the same, but on the other hand, they're not.
And going over here, there are hundreds of people.
I'm actually blown away.
But how many people came to this show
and it's not even everyone.
The different near clouds many times have a different angle,
like the thing they optimize on.
And they come from different backgrounds.
Some deliver best security.
Some deliver different kinds of accelerators.
Some deliver unique networks.
Some deliver better multi-tenancy.
So I think for the clouds, some deliver, by the way,
renewable energy or better access to energy.
A lot of them have a knack for what they think they do best.
I think the, and at this point there is such a big shortage.
Everyone's winning.
But I think in the long term, once we go through
the current hump, the ones that pick the right angle,
so not every product the market actually likes.
And you go to the supermarket, there are many brands
that deliver the same thing.
Not all of them are as popular
and it's not always easy to forecast who will.
But the near clouds that have the right differentiator
that customers want, that also are able to act
and deliver are the ones that will end up be winning.
>> So you've observed that there is actually a difference
between a near cloud that serves a single off-taker
as a tenant versus one that operates an independent cloud
that behave quite differently.
Can you tell us a little bit about that?
>> Yeah, so to begin with, they fund
in an entirely different way.
So the ones with a single off-taker
get that in a different way.
They first find the off-taker, then they go and use
that one for the underwriting.
And usually they end up being much more
capital efficient, capital effective.
But also the end price is way lower.
So if you're a single off-taker
and you think you can take everything
a near cloud can give you, you're going to get
a much better deal and I'm sure this is something
that you see at Silicon Data.
>> Yes.
>> When the near clouds that go
and they're going to market to the more general public
or the long tail, they are paying significantly more
for capital, which means from that moment on,
everything they're doing has to look fundamentally different
for their ends to meet.
Also it means that they need to use network technology,
storage technology, implemented in a way
that delivers very good separation across the customer.
So not only just access to funds is more expensive,
running their whole stack is more expensive.
So if you're a near cloud, you need to choose
what kind of a spending structure
and operational structure you want to do.
But definitely if you're an off-taker, you need to choose,
hey, do I think I may be big enough and stable enough
to commit for three or four or five years
on a large deployment, I can enjoy it.
Or unfortunately I cannot do it, I'm going to pay longer,
I'm going to pay more on a per usage.
>> That's really interesting.
So one last question, and this is something I looked up
before we come on, is you have this thing
called augmented memory grid.
And I was very curious about that.
I didn't have the chance to look up exactly what it is.
Would you tell us a little bit about it?
>> Yeah, so we started as at the storage company,
we've started with a product that delivered
the best parallel file system,
we then augmented with more protocols,
then we've added an object storage,
but that stays still within the storage realm.
Then we go and we looked at inference,
and we want to help our customers optimize inference.
Now, you can optimize inference
through a lot of different parameters,
you can use different decoding techniques,
you can use quantization,
you could deliver a different model.
So there are many, many ways of optimizing your compute.
But then one of the biggest questions is actually
how much of the work do you actually have to perform?
And how much of the work can you just reuse something
that you've already computed?
So with the augmented memory grid,
we're taking our incredibly low latency file system,
we're taking our GPU direct storage technology,
we're showing that we can push remote flash
to the GPU HBM as fast as NVIDIA is doing it
with their Dynamo from DRAM.
This is practically alchemy, like modern alchemy,
getting flash to work like DRAM.
And what we're doing, we're helping NeoClouds
or other inference service providers
to increase the cache efficiency.
And the better the cache efficiency,
the more tokens you deliver.
And the easiest example is let's say,
we are able to take you from 90% cache hit
to 98% cache hit.
On the 90%, it means that you're actually performing work,
100% of your GPUs perform work of 10% of the queries.
And this is how much data you're,
how much work you're able to do.
If you're caching 98%, it means that 100% of your GPUs
only have to work on 2%.
This is a five times difference.
And we're showing some of our customers,
we take them way higher than 98%.
So in that example, we just increased the token amount
that the same token factory delivers by five times.
So with augmented memory grid,
we're helping our customers leverage
a lot of the improvements on compute,
but really focus on getting as much of they can out of cache
and getting as little work done possible on the GPU
so they can deliver as many output tokens.
- Well, that's fascinating.
Thank you very much for that explanation.
I really learned a lot.
And thank you so much for stopping by.
Unfortunately, that's all the time we'll have for today.
But real, real pleasure to speak with you, Lauren.
And wish you excited and soon.
- Yeah, thank you very much, Steve.
I really enjoyed it.
